title: Controlling a stage: the progress review workshop
blurb: Explain the controlling a stage activities in agile terms, the progress review workshop and the project retrospective.
question: Midway through a stage, the project manager reviews stage progress, updates release map forecasts and checks which products users now own. Which activity is this, and in which workshop does it take place?

teach.body: Controlling a stage is where the project manager assigns work, monitors it, handles issues, reports progress to the board and takes corrective action so the stage stays within the board's tolerances. In agile, work is assigned as sets of user stories agreed with the product owner, progress is pulled from team dashboards, and the release map is kept up to date. The process normally starts after the project is authorized, but can also be used during initiation on large or complex projects.

head: Activity
Agile flavour
rows: Co-create the WPD with PO and team; update release map
Talk with the PO; pull from team dashboard
Confirm the user stories or timebox features
Review stage; update forecasts (in a progress review)
Update the project dashboard for the board to pull
Log and manage; seek board advice if needed
Options against canvas and release map; exception report
Choose a fix; trigger it via a work package
teach.caption: Paraphrased from Table 13.9.

teach.body: When something goes off track, the PM first checks the release map to see how far the stage has deviated. If the stage can stay within tolerance, the PM takes corrective action: gather information, pick the best option and trigger it by authorizing a work package. If tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, the PM assesses recovery options against the project canvas and release map and puts them, with a recommendation, to the board in an exception report.

Its purpose is to assess the project's current status, celebrate achievements and deal with challenges. By reviewing key metrics, accomplishments and open risks, the team and stakeholders reach a shared view of progress and agree mitigations. 'Evaluate stage status' takes place within a progress review, while activities such as authorizing a work package, escalating issues and risks and taking corrective action need no dedicated agile event.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.5.4.1, Tables 13.9 and 13.10

teach.body: Controlling a stage also has a project-level retrospective workshop. Its topics include the good (positive aspects of the project and key accomplishments), the learning (lessons and key takeaways), team building (a shared game, challenge or meal to strengthen relationships) and wrap-up (summarize outcomes and next steps). Risks are also gathered as a fixed part of team and project retrospectives.

At Redcliffe Leisure, project manager Aisha Bello agrees a set of booking-app user stories with product owner Liam Carter and his team. She pulls progress from their team dashboard and updates the release map. In the progress review, members try the new class booking screen in the product demo. When a payment supplier delay is forecast to push the stage beyond its time tolerance, Aisha sends the board an exception report with options and a recommendation.

teach.text: Within tolerance, the PM takes corrective action (via a work package); only a FORECAST breach of tolerance goes to the board in an exception report. And 'evaluate stage status' happens in a progress review, while the product demo shows the product, not the team's way of working.

items: Controlling a stage: assign, monitor, handle issues, report, correct within tolerance.
Can also be used during initiation on large or complex projects.
Progress pulled from team dashboards; board pulls from the project dashboard.
Corrective action via a work package; forecast breach goes in an exception report.
Progress review: welcome, highlights, risks and issues, product demo, wrap-up.
Project retrospective: the good, the learning, team building, wrap-up.

summary: You can now describe the controlling a stage activities in agile terms and the purpose and topics of the progress review workshop and project retrospective. You can also decide between corrective action and escalation.

A.q: In which controlling a stage activity does the PM pull progress from the updated team dashboard and update the release map with actuals and forecasts?
A.why: Evaluate work package status includes informal talks with the PO, pulling progress from the team dashboard and updating the release map (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Evaluate stage status reviews the whole stage in a progress review.
whyNot.1: Receiving a completed work package confirms the stories or features were delivered.
whyNot.3: Report highlights updates the project dashboard for the board.

A.q: Which controlling a stage activity takes place within a progress review?
A.why: Evaluate stage status takes place within a progress review (Table 13.9).

whyNot.1: Authorizing a work package needs no dedicated agile event.
whyNot.2: Corrective action needs no dedicated agile event.
whyNot.3: Escalation goes to the board in an exception report, not through a workshop.

A.q: What is the purpose of the progress review workshop?
options: To reflect on the last iteration and improve teamwork
To assess status, celebrate achievements and address challenges
To prepare the team plan for the next iteration
To plan the next stage and update the team OKRs
A.why: The progress review assesses the project's current status, celebrates achievements and addresses challenges (13.5.4.1).

whyNot.0: Reflecting on the last iteration is the team retrospective.
whyNot.2: The team plan comes from the team planning workshop.
whyNot.3: OKRs and next stage planning belong to the release planning workshop.

B.q: The PM forecasts that the stage will exceed its cost tolerance. Which activity applies, and which product goes to the board?
options: Take corrective action; a work package
Capture issues and risks; the daily log
Escalate issues and risks; an exception report
B.why: A forecast tolerance breach is escalated: the PM assesses options and recommends one to the board in an exception report (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Corrective action is for deviations the PM can fix within tolerance.
whyNot.1: The project dashboard reports routine progress, not a forecast breach.
whyNot.2: Capturing logs the issue; a forecast breach needs escalation.

B.q: In which activity does the PM update the project dashboard so that the board can pull the information it needs?
B.why: Report highlights assembles team dashboards, the project log and release map changes into the project dashboard for the board (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Evaluate stage status reviews progress and forecasts; reporting them is a separate activity.
whyNot.2: Receiving a work package confirms delivery of the agreed stories.
whyNot.3: Evaluating work package status pulls information from team dashboards.

B.q: The PM plans a team meal as part of a project retrospective. Under which topic does it belong?
B.why: Team building uses a shared game, challenge or meal to strengthen relationships (Table 13.11).

whyNot.1: The good shares positive aspects and accomplishments.
whyNot.2: The learning captures lessons and takeaways.
whyNot.3: Wrap-up summarizes outcomes and next steps.

C.q: A small deviation appears, but the stage can still finish within tolerance. What should the PM do, and how is the fix triggered?
options: Escalate it; through an exception report
Refer it to the board; in the project dashboard
Take corrective action; by authorizing a work package
Record it as a lesson; in the lessons log
C.why: Within tolerance the PM takes corrective action, triggered by authorizing a work package (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of tolerance.
whyNot.1: The board manages by exception; a deviation within tolerance stays with the PM.
whyNot.3: A lesson may be noted, but the deviation still needs corrective action.

C.q:
Which two statements about controlling a stage are correct?
1. It can be used during initiation for large or complex projects.
2. Each of its activities has a dedicated agile workshop.
3. Evaluate stage status takes place in a progress review.
4. The PM sends weekly written highlight reports instead of dashboards.
C.why: Controlling a stage can be used in initiation on large or complex projects (13.5.1), and evaluate stage status happens in a progress review (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: activities such as authorizing a work package need no dedicated agile event.
whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: activities such as taking corrective action need no dedicated agile event.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: several activities need no dedicated event, and the project dashboard replaces highlight reports.

C.q: In 'receive completed work package', what does the project manager confirm?
options: That the stage is within tolerance and the board is told
That the agreed user stories or timebox features were delivered
That the team has accepted the work package and its plan
That the release map has been approved for the next stage
C.why: The PM confirms the team has completed the work in the work package description (set of user stories) or delivered the features agreed for the timebox (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Stage tolerance is checked in evaluate stage status.
whyNot.2: Acceptance of the work package happens when it is authorized and accepted.
whyNot.3: The next stage's release map is approved by the board at a stage boundary.

reteach.title: Running a restaurant kitchen shift
reteach.question: How does a head chef 'control a stage' during a busy service?

blocks.body: The head chef hands tickets to each station, glances at the pass to see progress, fixes small problems by reassigning a dish, and calls the owner only if the night will clearly run over budget or time. Mid-shift, the team tastes plates together and talks about what is going well: a progress review with a demo.

blocks.text: The chef calls the owner for a forecast overrun, not for every small fix.

explain.body: Controlling a stage lets the PM assign and monitor work, handle issues, report progress and correct deviations so the stage stays within tolerance.

test.q: What is the purpose of controlling a stage?
options: To assign and monitor work and keep the stage within tolerance
To control the link between the PM and the delivery team
To give the board information to approve the next stage
To confirm that the project product has been accepted
test.why: That is the purpose of controlling a stage (13.5.1).

whyNot.2: That is managing a stage boundary.

explain.body: The PM co-creates and reviews the work package description (a set of user stories) with the PO and delivery team, confirms they accept it, authorizes work, reviews the team plan and updates the release map.

test.q: In 'authorize a work package', who co-creates and reviews the work package description with the PM?
options: The PO and the delivery team
test.why: The PM co-creates and reviews the WPD with the PO and the delivery team (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: The board authorizes stages, not work packages.
whyNot.1: The CPO prioritizes the project backlog; work packages are agreed with the PO's team.
whyNot.2: Project assurance monitors independently; it does not co-create work packages.

explain.body: After the welcome, project highlights reviews key metrics and accomplishments on the project dashboard, then open risks and issues are discussed and the product demo gathers user feedback.

test.q: Which progress review topic reviews key project metrics and accomplishments on the project dashboard?
test.why: Project highlights reviews metrics and accomplishments on the current project dashboard (Table 13.10).

whyNot.0: The welcome sets the agenda and introduces those present.
whyNot.1: The product demo shows completed features to users.
whyNot.3: Wrap-up summarizes outcomes and next steps.

explain.body: At project level, the retrospective covers the good, the learning, team building and wrap-up. Lessons and key takeaways are captured under the learning.

test.q: Under which project retrospective topic are lessons and key takeaways captured?
test.why: The learning captures lessons and key takeaways in group discussion (Table 13.11).

whyNot.0: The good shares positive aspects and accomplishments.
whyNot.3: Wrap-up summarizes outcomes and next steps.
